author: Danica Rachel
title: Protest called against October arms fair in Perth
content:
The Land Forces Exposition 2026, to be held at the Perth Convention and Exhibition Centre on 6-8 October, will be a three-day extravaganza of exhibitions, talks and luncheons, where the main topic of conversation is how best to kill people. More than 20,000 weapons company executives, politicians and military personnel from around the world are expected to attend.

We have to protest against this outrageous celebration of death and destruction.

Photos from the 2024 event on the front page of the 

Land Forces website

 are enough to make you ill. A smiling representative of Anduril, a company specialising in AI-powered warfare, shows off a battle drone. A live demonstration of a robot dog, presumably designed to carry autonomous weapons, takes place on the exhibition floor. A drone as big as a car hangs from the ceiling.

Lockheed Martin, the world’s biggest arms dealer—and builder of the F-35 fighter jets Israel uses to bomb Gaza—will have its latest death machines on display. As will Elbit Systems, Israel’s biggest weapons company.

Senior executives from Anduril and BAE Systems will speak on a panel discussing “the realities of Ukraine, Iran and other current conflicts”. Today’s bloodshed used as a case study to make tomorrow’s killing more efficient. What could those “other conflicts” be? Israel’s invasion of Lebanon? One assumes that there’s much these monsters have learn

author: James Plested
title: Victorian Socialists’ election campaign in full swing
content:
The Victorian state election will take place in just over two months, on Saturday 28 November. The Victorian Socialists’ campaign is now in full swing, with local campaign activity taking place daily across Melbourne and regional Victoria.

The scale of the campaign—with VS candidates set to run in all 88 lower house seats and all eight upper house regions across Victoria—is beyond anything the socialist left in Australia has attempted for generations (if ever). Even just a few years ago, a statewide campaign like this would have been unthinkable. That it’s happening at all is something of a breakthrough.

Between 1 June and 19 September, VS volunteers knocked on more than 80,000 doors, already well on track to reach the 2022 campaign total of around 190,000. The party received around 2,000 requests for campaign signs to be put on front fences and in yards, eclipsing the 2022 total of 1,000, with hundreds of orders a week still coming in. More than 2,400 people donated to the campaign, and almost 1,800 registered for a party event. 

New branches are springing up everywhere. Wherever they do, we’re finding people who want to get involved. VS events in places like Pakenham, a suburb on the far south-eastern fringe of Melbourne—more than 50 kilometres from the CBD—are attracting many new faces. And we now have active branches in regional centres including Geelong, Warrnambool, Ba

author: Tom Bramble
title: What’s the deal with productivity?
content:
The bosses are trying to convince workers that lower corporate taxes, fewer regulations and workers’ rights, and less union power would be good for real wages. What they really want is more profits at the expense of the working class.

For years, business lobby groups have decried what they call Australia’s “productivity crisis”. They don’t say workers are producing less than they used to; they say they aren’t increasing production as quickly as before and aren’t keeping pace with overseas productivity growth.

It’s true: growth in workers’ hourly output has slowed over the past decade, and Australian workers don’t produce as much value for the bosses as American workers. But the bosses argue that this means living standards are held back, and prices rise more than they otherwise would, contributing to the cost-of-living crisis.

They say that government regulations (rules about wages, hours of work, health and safety standards, construction standards, environmental protections and professional and occupational registration requirements) and trade unions are preventing business investment. Their solution is “deregulation”, “slashing red tape”, “more competition”. These are simply code words for attacking the working class.

Let’s break this down. First, what is productivity? The simplest definition is “output per hour”. For BlueScope Steel, it could be tonnes of steel produced

author: Emma Black
title: Strangulation: How did attempted murder become normal?
content:
A 16-year-old woman from Sydney’s northern beaches died in hospital in late August after reportedly being strangled during consensual sex with her partner. The tragedy has sparked a long-overdue reckoning with the consequences for young women of the pornification of sex and the normalisation of sexual violence that has come with it.

In recent years, sexual strangulation has gone from being a relatively marginal phenomenon to an everyday sexual practice. In Australia, 61 percent of young women report having been strangled during sex, according to a 

2024 survey

 of thousands of 18- to 35-year-olds. Men are most likely to be the stranglers. There is no safe way to strangle someone. According to David Corlett and Marie Crabbe, founders of anti-strangulation advocacy group Breathless:

“Potential 

consequences

 [of strangulation] 

range from

 neck pain to loss of bladder and bowel control, headaches, memory loss, seizures, brain damage, stroke and, as seems to be the case with the young woman from the northern beaches, death. The risks and consequences are cumulative, so the more someone is strangled, the more likely they are to suffer harm.”

Only a tiny percentage of middle-aged and older adults have engaged in sexual strangulation, but among young people it’s become commonplace. Maree Crabbe, who is also the director of 

It’s Time We Talked

, says strangulation wasn’t a

author: Lucy Chapman-Kelly
title: ‘Rig your own stages!’: Melbourne theatre workers strike
content:
Fans of Macy Gray were met by hundreds of Arts Centre Melbourne staff on strike for the first time in the institution’s history on 11 September. More than 95 percent of union members

 voted

 in favour of the 24-hour strike, rejecting management’s 3 percent offer and instead demanding an above-inflation pay rise, back pay from last October, and increased government funding for the arts.

According to the 

unions

 covering the workers—the Media, Entertainment and Arts Alliance and the Communications and Public Sector Union—Arts Centre staff wages have gone backwards in real terms by 10 percent since 2022, and almost 40 percent of the workforce is paid at the minimum award rate. Management’s 3 percent pay rise offer amounts to a further cut in real wages.

Nearly half the workforce is casual, and contact between workers is limited. Workers serving drinks at the bar, for example, might never interact with the ushers who seat people. The high turnover characteristic of casual work also means people don’t work with the same people consistently. This creates barriers to organising the workforce, and highlights why the strike, and the broader campaign for a better agreement, is a significant achievement.

For many of the workers, it was their first experience of an industrial campaign. Many brought handmade signs and gave impromptu speeches, with several pointing out that without t

author: Eleanor Morley
title: The problems of AI are the problems of capitalism
content:
Recent revelations about artificial intelligence models “going rogue” have raised serious concerns that the technology could soon cause great damage to human society. Already, the production and application of AI is wreaking havoc on the environment, amplifying existing social problems and expanding the powers of the surveillance state. While further regulation of the industry is necessary, the fundamental problem with AI is that capitalists control it and it is subject to the system’s prevailing conditions of profit maximisation, competition, imperial rivalry and more.

“The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade”, Jacob Coxon, a former researcher at Anthropic and OpenAI, the world’s leading frontier AI model developers, wrote on X in early September. Anthropic’s chief safety researcher Evan Hubinger later responded similarly. “We do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans”, he wrote. “I personally think it is >10 percent within the next decade.”

Amid the myriad other doomsday scenarios the world faces—catastrophic weather and mass extinction events from climate change, the threat of inter-imperialist nuclear war, economic collapse and mass starvation and so on—this latest warning of impending catastrophe could get lost. But it’s worth pausing to think about what exactly has just been said by people working at the frontier o

author: Ruby Healer
title: Labor doubles down on US military alliance
content:
“American force posture in Australia is growing”, Australian Defence Minister Richard Marles declared on his visit to Washington, DC, this month. “Since we’ve come to government”, Marles said, standing alongside US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, “you can see a through line there of growing American force posture in Australia”.

It was a fairly straightforward summary of the Albanese Labor government’s attitude, followed up with promises of further integration between the Australian and US militaries. A shifting “force posture” will mean more American troop rotations, more US air and naval operations and more pre-positioning of military equipment like warplanes, fuel and munitions in Australia.

Agreements made by the Albanese government will ramp up co-operation on all fronts, with a newly 

revitalised

 HMAS Stirling base near Perth set to host American nuclear-powered submarines and an estimated 2,300 US troops within five years. As America’s military machine looks ahead to an era of aggressive contest with China in the Asia-Pacific, Australia’s ruling class is desperate to make itself an indispensable part of US war planning.

Weapons trade regulations have also been 

loosened

 under a bilateral agreement to help both countries access shared research to develop arms and surveillance systems. And, Marles promised ominously, “you will hear more from us ... in the coming mon

author: James McVicar
title: Why do the Greens always chicken out?
content:
When Larissa Waters was elected leader of the Australian Greens, she said she was there to “

get shit done

”.

True to her word, Waters did something last week—and it was, indeed, shit. Greens MPs gave 

crucial support

 in the Senate to the roll-out of a carbon emissions offset scheme so bad that the term “greenwashing” seems generous.

Under the scheme, state governments will now be able to take publicly owned forest, promise not to deforest it, and then convert that promise into “carbon credits”. These credits can then be sold to greenhouse gas emitters to subtract from their overall carbon emissions count.

In NSW, the scheme is being tied to the establishment of a 476,000-hectare koala reserve the state government had already promised back in 2015. This move, according to Larissa Waters, put the Greens in an “

impossible position

” and forced them to support Labor’s carbon credit scam.

So now, in exchange for doing something it had already said it would do, the NSW Labor government can continue to do 

nothing

 to trees that were 

already there

 and, in turn, magically generate permits for carbon emitters to carry on emitting carbon.

The Greens are now trying to sell this as a step forward for the planet, Waters describing it as the “first chink in the armour of coal and gas”.

visual metaphor

 much nearer the mark, dep

author: Lance Selfa
title: Away from the cameras, Trump’s mass deportation campaign grinds on
content:
In the opening days of 2026, the Trump administration’s mass deportation operation faced a crisis, thanks to the brave resistance of ordinary people in Minnesota’s Twin Cities area. After Trump’s armed thugs murdered Renée Goode and Alex Pretti in broad daylight, when hundreds of cell phone videos refuted the Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem’s bald-faced slanders of the dead, the administration reset.

Trump fired Noem and cashiered Greg Bovino, a white supremacist Customs and Border Protection commander. Both Noem and Bovino had revelled in displays of immigration cops’ brutality and degradation of immigrants caught in their dragnets. They brought camera crews with them to create “content” of the terror campaign against immigrants for MAGA-aligned media.

Trump put “border czar” Tom Homan in charge of operations in Minnesota and then appointed Senator Markwayne Mullin to take over for Noem. These two dullards are no less committed to Trump’s anti-immigration agenda than were Noem and Bovino. But they have the good sense to keep themselves out of the limelight.

Trump suffered a political defeat in Minnesota. But in the months since, the mass deportation campaign has ground on. In fact, it may be achieving its aims more successfully while minimising social media images of armed goons terrorising neighbourhoods.

author: Anneke Demanuele
title: Ed Sheeran is a spineless twat
content:
“I just have a little message for you: there are two kinds of people in this world, Ed. There’re people who do the right thing—the rapper Macklemore would be one of those people. And there’re people—many of them, sadly little f ... excuse me, I nearly used the F-word then ... pricks—like you who do the wrong thing!”

So said Roger Waters, former Pink Floyd frontman and long-term supporter of the Palestinian people, via social media to singer Ed Sheeran, who has just committed a generational flop.

Bowing to the pressure of billionaires in a bid to stay “neutral”, Sheeran recently dropped rapper Macklemore from his 

Loop

 tour due to Macklemore’s pro-Palestine stance. In solidarity with Macklemore, all of the supporting artists, including Ed’s own band, dropped out of the tour.

The controversy began when billionaire New England Patriots stadium owner Robert Kraft phoned Sheeran with a clear demand: Macklemore would be removed from the show, or the show would not go on.

Macklemore drew the ire of Kraft after declaring his support for Palestine and performing his song “Hind’s Hall” at a concert at MetLife Stadium. “Hind’s Hall” was written when the campus encampments in solidarity with Gaza were at their height in the US. author: Connor Knight
title: Anti-Hanson students strike again
content:
The second high-school student strike against Pauline Hanson in as many months took place on 17 September, with thousands of students across the country downing pens and taking to the streets, defying principals and politicians alike.

More than 3,000 marched in Melbourne, while 1,000 took to the streets in each of Sydney, Adelaide and Perth. Hundreds rallied in Brisbane, Canberra and Hobart, and more walkouts occurred in regional areas than during the previous national day of action.

The chants this time were the same but carried more urgency, given Labor’s plans to restrict immigration. They included “Migrants are welcome, racists are not!” and “Unite, unite, unite to fight the right!” The mood was irreverent. Right-wing provocateurs were taunted, and in Brisbane, protesters climbed on urban art sculptures and rode skateboards with red flags in hand. In Melbourne, far-right troll Avi Yemeni was surrounded by chanting students, against whom his bodyguards weren’t much use.

The right-wing media response to the first walkout was as patronising as it was sensational. An 

Adelaide Now 

headline is typical: “Teen anti-Hanson rallies: are students really thinking for themselves?” Hanson herself was furious, accusing students of “hating this country”.

The wonderfully impertinent attitude of students in light of these insults and accusations was well captured by high-school socia

author: Editors
title: Labor capitulates to Hanson on migration
content:
The federal government’s new “

migration plan

”, announced by Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke on Thursday, is a spineless capitulation to One Nation’s constant attempts to blame migrants for Australia’s cost-of-living problems.

The primary targets in Labor’s plan are backpackers and international students. Who knew that these people, who pay thousands to be here—often for the privilege of doing crap, low-paid work—have been the problem all along.

Who isn’t the Labor Party targeting? Not the bankers squeezing billions from debt-laden workers. Not the supermarket duopoly with its fraudulent “sales” as it price fixes and gouges its way to multi-billion-dollar profits. Not the privatised aged care facilities that mint their owners untold millions every week while residents lie malnourished in their own excrement. Not the pokies venues and sports-betting companies making a killing from addicts.

Not the privatised utility companies taking a cut at every transmission point while pensioners freeze through winters and bake in summers to save power. Not the toll road operators given a license to print money off the back of commuters skipping meals so their kids can go on school excursions. Not the swarms of business owners who refuse to pay the legal minimum in wages and superannuation while their staff work two jobs.

Not the property developers and land bankers driving up housing

author: Anneke Demanuele
title: Albo is proud to be a houso—will anyone else get the chance?
content:
“I’m proud to be a houso, and I’m proud of the community in which I grew up.” These were the words of Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, spoken with a quivering top lip, after One Nation leader Pauline Hanson attacked his mother, Maryanne Albanese, for living most of her life in a public housing unit.

“Housing commission houses should not be there for people to live in them for 30, 40 [years]”, Hanson said. “And he said his mother lived in the same one she was born in for 65 years.”

Albanese may be proud to be a houso, but his party is ensuring that very few others will be able to access the level of housing security he and his mother did. Across the country, public housing is being eroded and depleted—homes and buildings left in disrepair, demolished or sold off to private developers. The idea that the government should build and provide long-term public housing to those who need it has been almost entirely destroyed.

In Victoria, public housing has been decimated. Walk-up estates have been bulldozed to make way for luxury developments, and 44 apartment towers are scheduled for demolition. The UN special rapporteur on adequate housing, Koldo Casla, has condemned the slated demolition of the 44 towers. In his letter to the Australian government, Casla writes:

author: Nick Reich
title: Largest strike of road transport workers in decades demands better pay and conditions
content:
The chants of several hundred striking truck drivers boomed from the steps of Victorian Trades Hall on the morning of 10 September: “When we fight, we win!”

The fight involves several workplaces around the country that united for a 24-hour strike. In Victoria, workers at FedEx, Border Express, K&S Chemtrans, Sadleirs and Qube all voted to take simultaneous action. Nationally, more than 5,000 workers walked off the job. The Transport Workers Union (TWU) officials claim that this strike is the largest road transport strike in Australian history.

Despite working for different companies, the issues striking truckers face are almost identical. Low wages, lack of job security and increasing pressures to do unsafe work. Across the industry, new companies increasingly undercut established, unionised companies by underpaying drivers and forcing them into higher-volume, unsafe work patterns. Road transport is no less essential than it was 30 years ago for the delivery of our food, fuel, medical supplies and other essentials, but over that time, the people driving the trucks have seen their wages go backwards and their working conditions become increasingly unsafe.

author: Deaglan Godwin
title: Another property developer collapses. We need to abolish them entirely
content:
The collapse of Bathla Group, a multi-billion-dollar property developer, illustrates how broken housing is in Australia.

Bathla entered voluntary administration in late August after it could no longer repay almost $3.4 billion in debt. Its collapse has left hundreds of workers unpaid and unemployed, and hundreds of buyers in limbo. The company owes millions to subcontractors and suppliers.

Bathla made immense profits from building dodgy houses and apartments in western Sydney. Harris Mazoudier, who purchased an apartment from Bathla in Schofields, spoke to the 

Sydney Morning Herald

 about the defects that littered his unit. Like many other property developers, Bathla has struggled to admit responsibility for these problems.

Profits also came from unsafe work practices. In 2015, a surveyor on a Bathla site fell nearly four metres and was impaled on concrete bars. SafeWork fined the company just $135,000 despite the surveyor’s long-term injuries. Industrial accidents are never treated with the same severity as criminal cases of the same magnitude.

Bathla’s founder, Bhart Bhushan, was once nicknamed “the Baron of Blacktown”. This appropriately sums up the power that property developers have over housing and urban planning. They wield this power to ensure the highest short-term profits, regardless of the social, economic and environmental consequences.
